lessons.title: Count Them All
lessons.concept: Joining Two Groups by Counting Every One

play.shortDesc: Touch every object in both groups to find how many there are altogether
play.targetObjective: Count both groups, one object at a time.
stepByStep: Look at the two groups.
Touch every object in the first group, then keep going into the second.
The last number you say is how many there are altogether.
play.kidTip: Do not start again at the second group. Keep counting on.
play.audioPrompt: Count them all! Touch every one in both groups to find how many altogether.

prompts.default: Count them all. How many altogether?

lessons.pedagogyTip: Counting all is where addition starts: a child who counts both groups from one is not behind, they are building the idea the shortcuts will later replace.

lessons.title: Put Them Together

play.shortDesc: Slide two groups into one pile, then count the pile
play.targetObjective: Put the two groups together, then count them.
stepByStep: Look at the two groups on their own.
Tap Put them together to make one pile.
Touch every object in the pile to count it.
play.kidTip: Adding means putting groups together. Then you count once.
play.audioPrompt: Put the two groups together, then count how many you have.

prompts.default: Put the groups together, then count them all.

lessons.pedagogyTip: Seeing two sets physically become one is what makes the plus sign mean something later.

lessons.title: Count On
lessons.concept: Starting from a Number Instead of from One

play.shortDesc: Hold the first number in your head and count on for the rest
play.targetObjective: Say the first number, then count on.
stepByStep: The first group is closed. Its number is written on the lid.
Say that number to yourself — you do not need to count it.
Touch the objects in the second group, counting on from there.
play.kidTip: The closed box is already counted. Start from its number.
play.audioPrompt: Count on! The first group is already counted, so start from its number.

prompts.default: Start at {a} and count on.

lessons.pedagogyTip: Counting on is the first real strategy: it treats the first number as a quantity rather than as something to be re-counted.

lessons.title: Start with the Bigger Number
lessons.concept: Counting On from the Larger Addend

play.shortDesc: Choose the bigger number to start from, so there is less to count
play.targetObjective: Start from the bigger number. It is less work.
stepByStep: Look at both numbers before you start.
Tap the bigger one to start from it.
Count on the smaller group — there are fewer to touch.
play.kidTip: You can add in any order, so start from the bigger number.
play.audioPrompt: Start with the bigger number! Then you have fewer to count on.

prompts.default: Start with the bigger number, then count on.

lessons.pedagogyTip: 3 + 8 and 8 + 3 give the same total, and one of them takes three counts instead of eight. That choice is the lesson.

lessons.title: Adding Zero

play.shortDesc: See that an empty group leaves the total exactly as it was
play.targetObjective: Adding zero leaves the number alone.
stepByStep: One group has objects. The other group is empty.
Nothing is being added, so nothing changes.
Choose the number you started with.
play.kidTip: Zero means none. The number stays the same.
play.audioPrompt: Adding zero! One group is empty, so what happens to the total?

prompts.default: What is {a} plus {b}?

lessons.pedagogyTip: Children who have only ever counted find zero genuinely strange — an empty group is still a group, and it still gets added.

lessons.title: Adding One
lessons.concept: One More Is the Next Number

play.shortDesc: Recognise that adding one just moves you to the next counting number
play.targetObjective: One more is the very next number.
stepByStep: Look at how many are in the big group.
One more is being added.
Say the next counting number — that is the answer.
play.kidTip: Adding one is just saying the next number.
play.audioPrompt: Adding one! One more is the next number you say when you count.

prompts.default: What is {a} plus {b}?

lessons.pedagogyTip: This is where the counting sequence stops being a song and starts being arithmetic: the number after seven *is* seven and one more.

lessons.title: Use Your Fingers
lessons.concept: Modelling Both Addends on Two Hands

play.shortDesc: Put one number on each hand, then count all the raised fingers
play.targetObjective: One number on each hand, then count them all.
stepByStep: Raise the first number of fingers on the left hand.
Raise the second number on the right hand.
Count every raised finger to find the total.
play.kidTip: One number on each hand. Then count every finger that is up.
play.audioPrompt: Use your fingers! Put one number on each hand, then count them all.

prompts.default: Show {a} on one hand and {b} on the other. How many fingers altogether?

lessons.pedagogyTip: Fingers are a manipulative a child always has. Discouraging them removes the model before the fact is known, which is what produces guessing.

lessons.title: Five Frame
lessons.concept: Adding Inside a Frame of Five

play.shortDesc: Add counters to a row of five and read the total without counting from one
play.targetObjective: Fill the frame, then read how many.
stepByStep: Some counters are already in the frame.
Tap empty spaces to add the rest.
The frame shows the total — you do not have to start again at one.
play.kidTip: The frame is already counted. Count on from the number in it.
play.audioPrompt: Five frame! Add counters to the row, then say how many there are.

prompts.default: Fill in {b} more. How many are there altogether?

lessons.pedagogyTip: Five is the first benchmark. A child who sees four as 'one less than five' has stopped counting one at a time.

lessons.title: Ten Frame
lessons.concept: Adding Inside a Frame of Ten

play.shortDesc: Add counters to two rows of five and read the total at a glance
play.targetObjective: Fill the frame, then read how many.
stepByStep: The top row holds five. The bottom row holds five more.
Tap empty spaces to add counters.
A full row of five helps you see the total without counting.
play.kidTip: A full top row is five. Count on from there.
play.audioPrompt: Ten frame! Add counters to the frame, then say how many altogether.

prompts.default: Fill in {b} more. How many are there altogether?

lessons.pedagogyTip: Two rows of five is what makes ten readable at a glance, and it is the structure every make-ten strategy later leans on.

lessons.title: Number Bonds

play.shortDesc: Read a bond diagram and give the whole that its two parts make
play.targetObjective: Two parts underneath make the whole on top.
stepByStep: The two boxes at the bottom are the parts.
The box at the top is the whole they make together.
Tap the empty box and type the whole.
play.kidTip: The two parts underneath make the whole on top.
play.audioPrompt: Number bonds! The two parts at the bottom make the whole at the top.

prompts.default: What do {a} and {b} make altogether?

lessons.pedagogyTip: A bond is the picture behind every later decomposition — breaking an addend, finding a missing part, and fact families are all this diagram with a different box blank.

lessons.title: The Number Path

play.shortDesc: Hop forward one square at a time and land on the answer
play.targetObjective: One hop is one number.
stepByStep: The marker starts on the first number.
Each hop moves it forward one square.
Say the number you land on. The last one is the answer.
play.kidTip: One hop is one number. Say each number as you land on it.
play.audioPrompt: The number path! Hop forward one square at a time and see where you land.

prompts.default: Start at {a} and hop forward {b}.

lessons.pedagogyTip: A path has one square per number, so hopping is counting made visible — this is where counting on stops being invisible mental work.

lessons.title: The Open Number Line

play.shortDesc: Take one jump on a line with no numbers, and work out where you landed
play.targetObjective: Nothing on this line tells you where you are.
stepByStep: Only the starting number is marked.
Take the jump — the arc stays on screen.
Work out where you landed and type it in.
play.kidTip: There are no numbers on this line, so keep the count in your head.
play.audioPrompt: The open number line! Take the jump, then work out where you landed.

prompts.default: Start at {a} and jump {b}. Where do you land?

lessons.pedagogyTip: An open line carries no answers, so it stops being a counting aid and becomes a place to record thinking — which is what makes it work for numbers too big to draw.

lessons.title: Base-Ten Blocks
lessons.concept: Adding with Tens and Ones You Can See

play.shortDesc: Build a two-digit answer out of ten-rods and one-units
play.targetObjective: Build the answer out of tens and ones.
stepByStep: Look at the two numbers you are adding.
Tap rods and units in the tray to drop them into the yard.
When the yard holds the answer, check it.
play.kidTip: Build each number out of blocks, then read what you have.
play.audioPrompt: Base-ten blocks! Build the answer out of ten-rods and one-units.

prompts.default: Build {a} plus {b} out of blocks.

lessons.pedagogyTip: A rod is worth ten because it is visibly ten units. A child who can check that is holding place value rather than remembering it.

lessons.title: The Place-Value Chart
lessons.concept: Adding One Column at a Time

play.shortDesc: Write two numbers in tens and ones columns and add each column
play.targetObjective: Ones go under ones. Tens go under tens.
stepByStep: Each number sits in its columns: tens on the left, ones on the right.
Add the ones column, then the tens column.
Write each answer in the column it belongs to.
play.kidTip: Add each column on its own. Ones with ones, tens with tens.
play.audioPrompt: The place-value chart! Add the ones column, then the tens column.

prompts.default: {a} plus {b}. Fill in the total, one column at a time.

lessons.pedagogyTip: Writing the digit in the right column is the skill. A chart that placed it for the child would be teaching something else.

lessons.title: Doubles

play.shortDesc: The Same Number Twice
play.targetObjective: A double is the same number twice.
stepByStep: Read the fact on the card.
Look at the two equal rows.
Type the total and check it.
play.kidTip: A double is the same number twice.
play.audioPrompt: Doubles! The same number twice — these are the facts to know by heart.

prompts.default: Double {a}. What is the total?

lessons.pedagogyTip: Doubles are learned as pictures rather than counted, and they are the anchor every near-double leans on afterwards.

lessons.title: Near Doubles: One More

play.shortDesc: A Double, and One More
play.targetObjective: A near double is one step from a double you already know.
stepByStep: Read the fact on the card.
Use the double it sits beside.
Type the total and check it.
play.kidTip: A near double is one step from a double you already know.
play.audioPrompt: Near doubles! This fact is one more than a double you know.

prompts.default: {a} plus {b}. It is one away from a double you know.

lessons.pedagogyTip: Naming the double first is the strategy. A child who jumps straight to the answer has not used it, even when they are right.

lessons.title: Near Doubles: One Less

play.shortDesc: A Double, and One Less
play.targetObjective: A near double is one step from a double you already know.
stepByStep: Read the fact on the card.
Use the double it sits beside.
Type the total and check it.
play.kidTip: A near double is one step from a double you already know.
play.audioPrompt: Near doubles! This fact is one less than a double you know.

prompts.default: {a} plus {b}. It is one away from a double you know.

lessons.pedagogyTip: Going down from a double is harder than going up, and worth its own lesson: the same relationship, the other direction.

lessons.title: Make Five

play.shortDesc: Say how many more counters a five-frame needs
play.targetObjective: Fill the frame right up. Count only the ones you put in.
stepByStep: Some counters are already in the frame.
Tap empty spaces until the frame is full.
The answer is how many you had to add — not the whole frame.
play.kidTip: Fill the frame right up. Count only the ones you put in.
play.audioPrompt: Make five! How many more counters does the frame need?

prompts.default: You have {a}. How many more to make {size}?

lessons.pedagogyTip: The answer is the part added, not the total. A child who says five has read the frame rather than the question.

lessons.title: Make Ten

play.shortDesc: Say how many more counters a ten-frame needs
play.targetObjective: Fill the frame right up. Count only the ones you put in.
stepByStep: Some counters are already in the frame.
Tap empty spaces until both rows are full.
The answer is how many you had to add.
play.kidTip: Fill the frame right up. Count only the ones you put in.
play.audioPrompt: Make ten! How many more counters does the frame need?

prompts.default: You have {a}. How many more to make {size}?

lessons.pedagogyTip: Friends of ten are the facts every bridging strategy stands on. Known instantly, they turn 8 + 5 into 10 + 3.

lessons.title: Reach the Next Ten

play.shortDesc: Choose the jump that lands exactly on the next ten
play.targetObjective: Jump to the round number, not past it.
stepByStep: Find the two tens your number sits between.
Work out how far it is to the one above.
Choose that jump — landing past it does not count.
play.kidTip: Jump to the round number, not past it.
play.audioPrompt: Reach the next ten! Which jump lands exactly on the round number?

prompts.default: Which jump takes {a} to the next ten?

lessons.pedagogyTip: Reaching the round number is the move inside every make-ten strategy. Practised alone, it stops being the hard part of 47 + 8.

lessons.title: Reach the Next Hundred

play.shortDesc: Choose the jump that lands exactly on the next hundred
play.targetObjective: Jump to the round hundred, not past it.
stepByStep: Find the two hundreds your number sits between.
Work out how far it is to the one above.
Choose that jump.
play.kidTip: Jump to the round hundred, not past it.
play.audioPrompt: Reach the next hundred! Which jump lands exactly on the round number?

prompts.default: Which jump takes {a} to the next hundred?

lessons.pedagogyTip: The same move one place up. A child who sees it as the same move has generalised; one who meets it as a new fact has not.

lessons.title: Break One Number Apart
lessons.concept: Splitting an Addend to Reach Ten

play.shortDesc: Split the second number so the first can reach ten
play.targetObjective: Give the first number just enough to reach ten, then add what is left.
stepByStep: Work out what the first number needs to reach ten.
Take that much out of the second number.
Whatever is left over is the other part.
play.kidTip: Give the first number just enough to reach ten, then add what is left.
play.audioPrompt: Break a number apart! Give the first one just enough to reach ten.

prompts.default: Break {b} apart so {a} can reach ten.

lessons.pedagogyTip: This is where make-ten becomes a strategy rather than a fact: the child chooses the split, and the split is the thinking.

lessons.title: Split Both Numbers

play.shortDesc: Break each two-digit number into its tens and its ones
play.targetObjective: Every two-digit number is some tens and some ones.
stepByStep: Look at the first number's tens and ones.
Write each part in its box — the tens as a whole ten.
Do the same for the second number.
play.kidTip: Every two-digit number is some tens and some ones.
play.audioPrompt: Split both numbers! Each one is some tens and some ones.

prompts.default: Split each number into its tens and its ones.

lessons.pedagogyTip: Splitting both is what makes adding by place possible. Writing forty rather than four is the part that has to be right.

lessons.title: Use a Fact You Know
lessons.concept: Deriving from a Fact You Hold

play.shortDesc: Pick the nearby fact that helps, then use it
play.targetObjective: Pick a fact you already know that is close to this one.
stepByStep: Look at the fact you have been given.
Choose the nearby fact you already know — a double is usually closest.
Count on or back from it to reach the answer.
play.kidTip: Pick a fact you already know that is close to this one.
play.audioPrompt: Use a fact you know! Which one is closest to this?

prompts.default: {a} plus {b}. Which fact would help?

lessons.pedagogyTip: Choosing the helper is the lesson. Every option offered is a real fact, so a child cannot pick well by spotting the silly one.

lessons.title: Fact Families

play.shortDesc: Write all four facts that three numbers make together
play.targetObjective: The same three numbers make four different facts.
stepByStep: Look at the three numbers in the family.
Two facts add them together, in either order.
Two facts take one part away from the whole.
play.kidTip: The same three numbers make four different facts.
play.audioPrompt: Fact families! The same three numbers make four different facts.

prompts.default: {a}, {b} and {sum} make a family. Fill in all four.

lessons.pedagogyTip: Seeing addition and subtraction as one family is what later makes a missing addend a question a child can answer.

lessons.title: Switch the Numbers
lessons.concept: Order Does Not Change the Total

play.shortDesc: Say the same fact the other way round
play.targetObjective: You can add in either order and the total does not change.
stepByStep: Read the fact you are given.
Say it the other way round — it starts with the other number.
The total is exactly the same.
play.kidTip: You can add in either order and the total does not change.
play.audioPrompt: Switch the numbers! The same fact the other way round makes the same total.

prompts.default: {a} plus {b}. Which is the same fact the other way round?

lessons.pedagogyTip: Commutativity is what makes starting from the larger number allowed. Stated as its own idea, it stops being a trick.

lessons.title: Friendly Pairs

play.shortDesc: Spot the two numbers that make ten and add those first
play.targetObjective: Look for two that make ten and put those together first.
stepByStep: Look across all the numbers, not just the first two.
Find the two that make ten and tap them together.
Add what is left to the ten.
play.kidTip: Look for two that make ten and put those together first.
play.audioPrompt: Friendly pairs! Two of these make ten. Find them first.

prompts.default: Two of these make {target}. Put those together first.

lessons.pedagogyTip: Order is a choice once there are more than two numbers, and finding the ten first is what makes the rest easy. This is commutativity put to work.

lessons.title: Give and Take Back

play.shortDesc: Add an easy round number, then give back what you took too much of
play.targetObjective: Jump a round number, then give back what you took too much of.
stepByStep: Notice the second number is nearly a round one.
Jump the round number instead — it is much easier.
Then jump back the little bit you overshot by.
play.kidTip: Jump a round number, then give back what you took too much of.
play.audioPrompt: Give and take back! Add the easy round number, then give back the extra.

prompts.default: {a} plus {b}. Jump a round number, then give back what you overshot.

lessons.pedagogyTip: Compensation is the first strategy that makes a problem temporarily wrong on purpose. Seeing the overshoot on the line is what makes that safe.

lessons.title: Adding Tens

play.shortDesc: Add whole tens by building the answer out of rods
play.targetObjective: Adding tens is like adding ones, only bigger.
stepByStep: Both numbers are whole tens, so only rods are offered.
Count the rods you need and drop them in.
Three rods and four rods is seven rods — seventy.
play.kidTip: Adding tens is like adding ones, only bigger.
play.audioPrompt: Adding tens! Three tens and four tens is seven tens.

prompts.default: {a} plus {b}. Build the answer out of tens.

lessons.pedagogyTip: Once ten is a unit, adding tens is the same work as adding ones. That transfer is the point, and it is why the rods are all the tray offers.

lessons.title: Adding Hundreds

play.shortDesc: Add whole hundreds by building the answer out of flats
play.targetObjective: Adding hundreds is the same move, one place up.
stepByStep: Both numbers are whole hundreds, so only flats are offered.
Count the flats you need.
Three flats and four flats is seven flats — seven hundred.
play.kidTip: Adding hundreds is the same move, one place up.
play.audioPrompt: Adding hundreds! The same move as adding tens, one place up.

prompts.default: {a} plus {b}. Build the answer out of hundreds.

lessons.pedagogyTip: A child who meets this as the same move has generalised the unit idea; one who meets it as a new fact has not.

lessons.title: Tens, Then Ones

play.shortDesc: Take one big jump of tens and then a small one of ones
play.targetObjective: Add the tens first, then the ones.
stepByStep: Break the second number into its tens and its ones.
Jump the tens — it is one big, easy jump.
Then jump the ones, and say where you landed.
play.kidTip: Add the tens first, then the ones.
play.audioPrompt: Tens then ones! One big jump, then a small one.

prompts.default: {a} plus {b}. Jump the tens, then the ones.

lessons.pedagogyTip: Two jumps instead of one is what makes a two-digit addition manageable in the head, and the open line is where that becomes visible.

lessons.title: Hundreds, Tens and Ones

play.shortDesc: Add three-digit numbers one column at a time
play.targetObjective: Add each column on its own. Ones with ones, tens with tens.
stepByStep: Each number fills three columns now.
Add the ones, then the tens, then the hundreds.
Write each answer under the column it came from.
play.kidTip: Add each column on its own. Ones with ones, tens with tens.
play.audioPrompt: Hundreds, tens and ones! Add each column on its own.

prompts.default: {a} plus {b}. Fill in the total, one column at a time.

lessons.pedagogyTip: A third column adds no new idea, which is exactly what a child should discover: the method already worked.

lessons.title: Expanded Form
lessons.concept: Writing a Number as Its Parts

play.shortDesc: Write each number as hundreds plus tens plus ones, then add
play.targetObjective: Every number is some hundreds, some tens and some ones.
stepByStep: Each number is written out as the values it is made of.
Add the hundreds together, then the tens, then the ones.
Write each column's answer as its full value — forty, not four.
play.kidTip: Every number is some hundreds, some tens and some ones.
play.audioPrompt: Expanded form! Write each number as hundreds, tens and ones.

prompts.default: {a} plus {b}, written out in hundreds, tens and ones.

lessons.pedagogyTip: Writing forty rather than four is the whole difficulty. Expanded form makes the value of a digit impossible to ignore.

lessons.title: Partial Sums

play.shortDesc: Add each column, keep both answers, then put them together
play.targetObjective: Add one column at a time, and keep each answer before putting them together.
stepByStep: Add the tens and write that answer down.
Add the ones and write that one down too.
Put the two answers together for the total.
play.kidTip: Add one column at a time, and keep each answer before putting them together.
play.audioPrompt: Partial sums! Add each column, keep both answers, then add those.

prompts.default: {a} plus {b}. Add the tens, add the ones, then put them together.

lessons.pedagogyTip: Nothing is carried here — the partials do that job in the open, which is why this comes before the algorithm that hides it.

lessons.title: Left to Right

play.shortDesc: Start with the biggest column and let each one after it adjust the total
play.targetObjective: Start with the biggest column, then let each one after it change the number you are holding.
stepByStep: Add the tens first and hold that number.
Add the ones to the number you are holding.
You never write two answers down — only the one that grows.
play.kidTip: Start with the biggest column, then let each one after it change the number you are holding.
play.audioPrompt: Left to right! Start with the tens and let the ones change what you are holding.

prompts.default: {a} plus {b}. Start with the biggest column and work right.

lessons.pedagogyTip: This is how most people add in their heads, and it is worth naming: one number that grows, rather than parts collected and totalled at the end.

lessons.title: Trade Ten Ones

play.shortDesc: Bundle ten loose ones into a single ten-rod
play.targetObjective: Ten of one block always becomes one of the next block up.
stepByStep: Both numbers are already tipped into the yard.
The ones column holds more than nine — that cannot stay.
Bundle ten of them into one rod, then read the answer.
play.kidTip: Ten of one block always becomes one of the next block up.
play.audioPrompt: Trade ten ones! Ten loose ones become a single ten.

prompts.default: {a} plus {b}. Bundle ten ones into a ten, then read the answer.

lessons.pedagogyTip: The exchange comes before the algorithm on purpose: carrying is this move written small, and a child who has done it can read the little one.

lessons.title: Trade Ten Tens

play.shortDesc: Bundle ten ten-rods into a single hundred-flat
play.targetObjective: Ten of one block always becomes one of the next block up.
stepByStep: The tens column holds more than nine rods.
Bundle ten rods into one flat.
Then read what the yard holds.
play.kidTip: Ten of one block always becomes one of the next block up.
play.audioPrompt: Trade ten tens! Ten rods become a single hundred.

prompts.default: {a} plus {b}. Bundle ten tens into a hundred, then read the answer.

lessons.pedagogyTip: The same move one place up. A child who sees it as the same move will not be surprised when a column carries twice.

lessons.title: Two Carries
lessons.concept: A Carry That Makes Another Carry

play.shortDesc: Work a column sum where the carry itself causes a second carry
play.targetObjective: Start at the ones. When a column makes ten or more, write the carry above the next one.
stepByStep: Add the ones. Write the carry above the tens.
Add the tens — including the carry — and it reaches ten as well.
Write that carry above the hundreds and finish.
play.kidTip: Start at the ones. When a column makes ten or more, write the carry above the next one.
play.audioPrompt: Two carries! One column carries, and that makes the next one carry too.

prompts.default: {a} plus {b}. Two columns carry — write each one down.

lessons.pedagogyTip: The carry that causes another carry is where children lose the thread. Meeting it as its own lesson beats meeting it by accident.

lessons.title: The Written Method
lessons.concept: The Compact Form of Everything Before It

play.shortDesc: Add in columns with a single carry, the way it is written down
play.targetObjective: Start at the ones. When a column makes ten or more, write the carry above the next one.
stepByStep: Add the ones column first.
If it reaches ten, write the small one above the tens.
Add the tens, including the carry.
play.kidTip: Start at the ones. When a column makes ten or more, write the carry above the next one.
play.audioPrompt: The written method! Start at the ones and write the carry above the next column.

prompts.default: {a} plus {b}. Add each column, and write the carry.

lessons.pedagogyTip: Everything earlier folded into one procedure. The only thing kept on paper is the carry, which is why it is not optional here.

lessons.title: Three or More

play.shortDesc: Add a list of numbers in whatever order is easiest
play.targetObjective: Add them in whatever order is easiest — the total is the same.
stepByStep: Look at all the numbers before you start.
Tap two to put them together, and keep going.
The order you choose does not change the total.
play.kidTip: Add them in whatever order is easiest — the total is the same.
play.audioPrompt: Three or more! Add them in whatever order suits you best.

prompts.default: Add these in whatever order is easiest.

lessons.pedagogyTip: With three numbers, order becomes a decision rather than a given. That freedom is what every later shortcut is built on.

lessons.title: Compatible Numbers

play.shortDesc: Find both pairs that make ten before adding what is left
play.targetObjective: Find every pair that makes ten first, then add the rest.
stepByStep: There is more than one friendly pair hiding here.
Put each pair together before you add anything else.
Two tens and a leftover is an easy sum.
play.kidTip: Find every pair that makes ten first, then add the rest.
play.audioPrompt: Compatible numbers! More than one pair makes ten. Find them all.

prompts.default: Find the pairs that make {target}, then add the rest.

lessons.pedagogyTip: Scanning a whole list for what fits together — rather than working left to right — is the habit this lesson is really after.

lessons.title: Keep a Running Total

play.shortDesc: Add one number at a time, writing the total as you go
play.targetObjective: Keep the total in your head and add the next one to it.
stepByStep: Start with the first number.
Add the second, and write what you are holding.
Keep going — each answer feeds the next.
play.kidTip: Keep the total in your head and add the next one to it.
play.audioPrompt: Keep a running total! Add one number at a time and hold the answer.

prompts.default: Add them one at a time, keeping the total as you go.

lessons.pedagogyTip: A running total is how a long list is actually added. Writing each step makes the place a mistake entered findable.

lessons.title: About How Many

play.shortDesc: Round each number to the nearest ten, then add the round numbers
play.targetObjective: Round each number to the nearest one, then add the round numbers.
stepByStep: Each number sits between two tens.
Choose the one it is nearer to.
Add the two round numbers — that is about how many.
play.kidTip: Round each number to the nearest one, then add the round numbers.
play.audioPrompt: About how many? Round each number first, then add the round ones.

prompts.default: About how many is {a} plus {b}?

lessons.pedagogyTip: The exact answer is not wanted here, and a child who gives it has answered a different question. The prompt says about, and so does the feedback.

lessons.title: Could That Be Right?
lessons.concept: Judging an Answer Without Working It Out

play.shortDesc: Decide whether someone's answer is close, far too big, or far too small
play.targetObjective: You do not need the exact answer. Ask whether it is anywhere near.
stepByStep: Round both numbers to see roughly where the answer should be.
Compare that with the answer you were given.
Say whether it is about right, far too big, or far too small.
play.kidTip: You do not need the exact answer. Ask whether it is anywhere near.
play.audioPrompt: Could that be right? Work out roughly where the answer should be.

prompts.default: Someone says {a} plus {b} is {claim}. Could that be right?

lessons.pedagogyTip: Checking an answer without recomputing it is what stops a slipped digit going unnoticed, and it is a habit rather than a fact.

lessons.title: The Missing Part
lessons.concept: Finding a Part When the Whole Is Known

play.shortDesc: Work out the part that is missing from a number bond
play.targetObjective: The two parts have to make the whole. One is missing.
stepByStep: The whole is at the top and one part is already there.
Count on from the part you can see until you reach the whole.
However far you counted is the missing part.
play.kidTip: The two parts have to make the whole. One is missing.
play.audioPrompt: The missing part! One part is hidden. What goes with the other to make the whole?

prompts.default: {sum} is the whole. What is the missing part?

lessons.pedagogyTip: A missing addend is where addition and subtraction meet. A child who has done fact families already has the tool.

lessons.title: Getting More

stories: {name} had {a} {thing}. Then {name} found {b} more. How many {thing} now?
{name} picked {a} {thing} on Monday and {b} more on Tuesday. How many altogether?
There were {a} {thing} in the box. {other} put in {b} more. How many now?

play.shortDesc: Model a story where something is added, then find the new total
play.targetObjective: Both parts are known. The bar asks for the whole.
stepByStep: Read the story — or tap the speaker to hear it.
Put each number the story gives you into its box.
The empty box is what you are asked for.
play.kidTip: Both parts are known. The bar asks for the whole.
play.audioPrompt: Getting more! Something is added — how many are there now?

prompts.default: {text}

lessons.pedagogyTip: The simplest story type, and the one that makes the bar model worth trusting before the harder types need it.

lessons.title: Two Kinds, One Total

stories: {name} has {a} red {thing} and {b} blue {thing}. How many {thing} altogether?
There are {a} big {thing} and {b} small {thing} in the jar. How many is that?
{name} has {a} {thing} and {other} has {b}. How many do they have together?

play.shortDesc: Model a story where two groups are counted together
play.targetObjective: Nothing changes here — two groups are simply counted together.
stepByStep: Read the story.
Put each group into its own box.
The whole is what you are asked for.
play.kidTip: Nothing changes here — two groups are simply counted together.
play.audioPrompt: Two kinds, one total! Two groups counted together.

prompts.default: {text}

lessons.pedagogyTip: Nothing moves in a part-part-whole story, which is what makes it different from a join even though the arithmetic is identical.

lessons.title: How Many More?

stories: {name} had {a} {thing}. Now {name} has {b}. How many more did {name} get?
There were {a} {thing} in the box. Now there are {b}. How many were put in?
{name} started with {a} {thing} and ended with {b}. How many did {name} collect?

play.shortDesc: Model a story where the total is known but the change is not
play.targetObjective: You know where it started and where it ended. The middle is missing.
stepByStep: Read the story — the total is already known.
Put the starting number in its box.
The empty box is how many were added.
play.kidTip: You know where it started and where it ended. The middle is missing.
play.audioPrompt: How many more? You know the start and the end — find what was added.

prompts.default: {text}

lessons.pedagogyTip: The same three numbers as a join, with a different one missing. Which box is empty is the entire difficulty.

lessons.title: Where Did It Start?

stories: {name} found {a} more {thing}. Now {name} has {b}. How many {thing} did {name} start with?
{other} gave {name} {a} {thing}. Now {name} has {b}. How many did {name} have before?
{a} {thing} were added to the box. Now there are {b}. How many were there first?

play.shortDesc: Model a story where the ending is known but the beginning is not
play.targetObjective: You know what was added and where it ended. The start is missing.
stepByStep: Read the story — the total is known.
Put the number that was added into its box.
The empty box is what there was to begin with.
play.kidTip: You know what was added and where it ended. The start is missing.
play.audioPrompt: Where did it start? You know what was added and what there is now.

prompts.default: {text}

lessons.pedagogyTip: The hardest of the addition types: the story runs forward and the thinking runs backward, and only the bar makes that safe.

lessons.title: How Many Altogether?

stories: {name} has {a} {thing}. {other} has {b} more than {name}. How many does {other} have?
{name} collected {a} {thing}. {other} collected {b} more. How many did {other} collect?

play.shortDesc: Model a story where one person has a number more than another
play.targetObjective: Two bars, lined up. The longer one is the smaller amount plus the difference.
stepByStep: Read the story — someone has more than someone else.
Build the shorter bar, then match it on the longer one.
Add the extra to find the bigger amount.
play.kidTip: Two bars, lined up. The longer one is the smaller amount plus the difference.
play.audioPrompt: How many altogether? One has more than the other — how many is that?

prompts.default: {text}

lessons.pedagogyTip: A comparison is two bars rather than one, and lining them up is what turns 'more than' from words into a length.

lessons.title: Two Steps

stories: {name} had {a} {thing}. {other} gave {name} {b} more, and then {c} more. How many now?
There were {a} {thing} in the jar. {name} added {b}, then {other} added {c}. How many now?

play.shortDesc: Work a story that changes twice, one step at a time
play.targetObjective: Answer the first change, then carry that answer into the second.
stepByStep: Read the whole story before you start.
Work out where things stood after the first change.
Then carry that number into the second change.
play.kidTip: Answer the first change, then carry that answer into the second.
play.audioPrompt: Two steps! Something changes twice — take it one change at a time.

prompts.default: {text}

lessons.pedagogyTip: Two steps is where children stop and answer the first question as if it were the last. Asking for the middle number on purpose is what stops that.

lessons.title: Which Way Is Best?
lessons.concept: Choosing a Strategy, and Saying Why

play.shortDesc: Pick a strategy that suits the numbers, then see which route was shorter
play.targetObjective: More than one way is right. Some ways are shorter than others.
stepByStep: Look at the two numbers before you choose anything.
Pick a strategy that suits them — more than one may.
Then compare two routes and count the steps each one took.
play.kidTip: Look at the numbers before you choose. Some strategies only suit some numbers.
play.audioPrompt: Which way is best? Look at the numbers, then choose how you would add them.

prompts.default: {a} plus {b}. Which strategy would you use?

lessons.pedagogyTip: The only lesson here with more than one right answer. A child who can say why a strategy suits these numbers has stopped following recipes and started choosing.

lessons.title: Practice: Frames

play.shortDesc: Four frame techniques mixed together, with nothing to lean on.
play.targetObjective: No hints, no explanations, no voice. Just the questions.
stepByStep: The techniques you have learned, mixed together.
Nothing is read aloud and there are no hints.
Work each one out, and see how many you get first time.

lessons.pedagogyTip: Practice is retrieval, not instruction. The help is removed on purpose — recalling a technique unaided is a different act from being walked through it, and it is the one that makes it stick.
